title: Can Faith Be a Science? Aquinas on Borrowed First Principles
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Summa Theologiae, First Part, Question 1: The nature and extent of sacred doctrine
source.authors: St. Thomas Aquinas (literally translated by Fathers of the English Dominican Province)
source.venue: The Summa Theologiæ of St. Thomas Aquinas, Second and Revised Edition (online edition, New Advent)

intro.summary: Thomas Aquinas, a 13th-century friar and teacher, opens his great textbook of theology by asking what kind of knowledge theology is. Is it needed at all, given philosophy? Can it be a 'science', a body of knowledge reasoned out from first principles, when those principles are taken on faith? Working through objections and replies, he argues that a teaching revealed by God is needed. He then argues that it is a genuine science because, like music borrowing its principles from arithmetic, it reasons from principles supplied by a higher knowledge. The main limitation is that the argument works only from inside a faith commitment: it shows how theology could be a science if its principles really are revealed, not that they are.
background: Thomas Aquinas (about 1225–1274) was a Dominican friar who wrote the Summa Theologiae as a textbook for students of theology.

In his time 'science' (Latin scientia) meant any organized body of knowledge that draws conclusions by strict reasoning from first principles, an idea taken from Aristotle. It did not mean laboratory experiment.
'Sacred doctrine' is Aquinas's name for teaching based on what he holds God has revealed, mainly in Scripture. Today we would roughly call it theology.
Each 'article' of the Summa is a small structured debate: objections first, then a contrary authority, then Aquinas's own answer, then replies to each objection.
intro.aha: Aquinas claims that theology counts as a real science even though its starting points cannot be proved by reason, because every science starts from unproved principles, and some sciences, like music relying on arithmetic, simply borrow theirs from a higher one.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Before teaching theology, Aquinas asks whether it should exist at all. Philosophy already uses human reason to study everything that exists, even God. So why would anyone need a further kind of knowledge on top of philosophy?
primer.quote: It seems that, besides philosophical science, we have no need of any further knowledge.

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: Aquinas works through ten short debates, called articles. Each one first states the strongest objections against his view. Then it cites a contrary authority, gives his own answer, and replies to each objection in turn. He asks whether this teaching is needed, whether it is a science, whether it is one science, how it uses argument and metaphor, and how Scripture should be read.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: He argues that revelation is needed for two reasons. Some truths lie beyond reason. Even the truths about God that reason can reach would otherwise be found by only a few people, late in life, and mixed with errors. His most surprising move is to call this teaching a true science even though its starting points cannot be proved. A musician also takes his principles on trust from the mathematician, and theology takes its principles from God's own knowledge.
primer.quote: So it is that sacred doctrine is a science because it proceeds from principles established by the light of a higher science, namely, the science of God and the blessed.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: The text shaped centuries of debate about how faith and reason relate. It also gives a careful picture of how any field rests on starting points it does not prove itself. But the argument assumes from the start that its principles come from God. A reader who does not share that faith can still follow the logic without accepting the premises. Here we read an English translation from 1920 of a medieval Latin text, so some key words, such as 'science', do not mean what they mean today.

concepts.title: How an article argues: objections first
concepts.idea: Each article is a mini-debate that states the opposing view at its strongest, cites a contrary authority, gives an answer, and then replies to each objection one by one.

terms.means: An argument for the view Aquinas will reject, opening with 'It seems that…' and put as strongly as he can
A short appeal to an authority, such as Scripture or a respected writer, that points the other way from the objections
The body of the article, where Aquinas gives his own position and his reasons
A closing answer to one objection, often granting what is right in it and showing why it still fails

concepts.recap: Read an article as a debate in five moves: question, objections, a contrary authority, Aquinas's answer, then replies that settle each objection. His own view is in 'I answer that'.

understand.explanation: Each article in the Summa is built like a small, staged debate. It poses a yes-or-no question, then lets the other side speak first, in objections that begin 'It seems that…'. A single contrary authority follows, marked 'On the contrary'. Then comes 'I answer that', where Aquinas sets out his own position and his reasons. Last, each reply to objection returns to one objection by number. It often grants what is true in that objection and shows why it does not overturn the answer. So the first thing you read is usually what he will reject, and his own view is found in 'I answer that' and the replies.
understand.quote: Reply to Objection 1. Although those things which are beyond man's knowledge may not be sought for by man through his reason, nevertheless, once they are revealed by God, they must be accepted by faith.

activities.prompt: Here is Article 1 of the Summa, one part at a time. For each part, notice what job it does in the debate.

stages.label: 1. The question
stages.text: The article opens with one yes-or-no question: 'Whether, besides philosophy, any further doctrine is required?' In other words: is human reasoning (philosophy) enough, or do we also need teaching that God reveals?

stages.label: 2. Objections
stages.text: Aquinas does not begin with his own view. He begins with the other side, and each argument opens with 'It seems that…'. Objection 1 says we should not seek what is above reason, and whatever is not above reason is already covered by philosophy. Objection 2 says philosophy studies everything that exists, even God. These are called objections. They are put strongly because they are the arguments he must defeat.

stages.label: 3. On the contrary
stages.text: Next comes one short appeal to authority that points the other way. Here it is 2 Timothy 3:16: Scripture inspired by God is 'profitable to teach'. Since Scripture is not part of philosophy, some knowledge beyond philosophy is useful. This 'on the contrary' only shows that the question is truly open. It is not yet the full argument.

stages.label: 4. I answer that
stages.text: Now Aquinas speaks for himself: 'I answer that, It was necessary for man's salvation that there should be a knowledge revealed by God besides philosophical science built up by human reason.' He then gives his reasons, which the next concept examines. This part is his own position.

stages.label: 5. Replies to the objections
stages.text: Last, he goes back to each objection by number. Each part is headed 'Reply to Objection 1', 'Reply to Objection 2', and so on. In the reply to objection 1 he grants its point: reason should not pry into what is beyond it. Then he adds that once such things are revealed, they are accepted by faith. The reply to objection 2 answers with a distinction about how sciences differ, which a later concept covers. No objection is left unanswered.

activities.takeaway: Every article moves the same way: question, objections, a contrary authority, Aquinas's answer, then a reply to each objection.

activities.prompt: Put these pieces of Article 1 into the order in which they appear.
items: Whether, besides philosophy, any further doctrine is required?
It seems that, besides philosophical science, we have no need of any further knowledge.
On the contrary, Scripture inspired by God is 'profitable to teach', and it is no part of philosophy.
I answer that, it was necessary for salvation that there be knowledge revealed by God besides philosophy.
Reply to Objection 1: things beyond reason may not be sought by reason, but once revealed they are accepted by faith.
activities.explanation: The question comes first. The opposing view follows ('It seems that…'), then the contrary authority. Aquinas's own answer comes next, and the replies close the article by going back over the objections. The objections must come before the answer because the replies at the end refer to them by number.
hints: Which piece is phrased as a question rather than a claim?
'It seems that…' always marks the side Aquinas will argue against, and it comes early.
A reply can only answer an objection that has already been stated, so the replies come last.

activities.question: In Article 1, which part tells you Aquinas's own position on the question?

options.text: Objection 1, because it comes first
options.feedback: Coming first does not make it his view. 'It seems that…' introduces the opposing side, the one he goes on to reject.

options.text: On the contrary, because it quotes Scripture
options.feedback: This part cites one authority against the objections and shows the question is open. It is not where Aquinas argues his case. In some articles it does not even match his final view exactly.

options.text: I answer that
options.feedback: Correct. This is the body of the article. Here Aquinas states that revealed knowledge was necessary besides philosophy, and he gives his reasons.

options.text: Reply to Objection 2
options.feedback: The replies defend the answer against each objection, so they show his view at work. But they rely on the position already set out in 'I answer that'. They do not state it in full.

hints: Which part is written in Aquinas's own voice from the start: 'I…'?

activities.question: Article 4 asks whether sacred doctrine is a practical science. Its 'On the contrary' ends: 'Therefore it is not a practical but a speculative science.' The 'I answer that' says sacred doctrine 'includes both', though 'it is speculative rather than practical'. What does this show about the structure?

options.text: The 'On the contrary' is only a counterweight to the objections. The final, more careful position is in 'I answer that'.
options.feedback: Correct. The contrary authority pushes against the objections, which said 'practical'. But Aquinas's own answer is more nuanced: it covers both kinds of science and leans toward speculative. Always read the answer, not just the 'On the contrary'.

options.text: Aquinas contradicts himself between the two parts.
options.feedback: No. The 'On the contrary' is not his considered answer, so there is nothing to contradict. It balances the objections. His answer then refines the question rather than simply picking a side.

options.text: The objections were right after all, since sacred doctrine is partly practical.
options.feedback: Partly, and that is the point. Aquinas grants that it treats human acts, so the objections have something true in them. But he concludes that it is speculative rather than practical, so the objections' claim that it is a practical science still fails.

hints: Compare how strong each part's claim is: 'not a practical' versus 'includes both… rather than'.

concepts.title: Two reasons reason is not enough
concepts.idea: Revelation is needed both for truths beyond reason and for truths reason could reach but would reach only for a few, late, and with errors.

terms.means: Knowledge that God makes known to people, as opposed to knowledge they work out by their own reasoning
Aquinas's name for all the knowledge human reason builds up on its own, including reasoning about God
For Aquinas, reaching God as the final goal of human life; he holds that this depends on knowing truths about God

concepts.recap: Aquinas gives two reasons for revelation: some truths lie beyond reason, and the truths reason can reach would reach only a few, late, and mixed with errors.

understand.explanation: In the answer section of Article 1, Aquinas gives two separate reasons why human reasoning alone (philosophical science) is not enough. First, people are directed toward a goal, God, that is beyond what reason can grasp, and you must know a goal before you can steer toward it, so some truths have to be revealed. Second, even truths about God that reason could in principle work out would, left to reason alone, be known by only a few people, only after a long time, and mixed with many errors. Since he holds that salvation depends on this knowledge, he concludes it should also be taught by revelation, so that more people know it sooner and more surely. The argument rests on premises he takes from faith, such as that human life is directed to God. The 'few, late, with errors' point is a general claim about how human thinking goes, not something he measures.
understand.quote: Hence it was necessary for the salvation of man that certain truths which exceed human reason should be made known to him by divine revelation. Even as regards those truths about God which human reason could have discovered, it was necessary that man should be taught by a divine revelation;

activities.prompt: Article 1 asks whether people need any knowledge besides what human reasoning builds up on its own. Aquinas calls that home-made knowledge 'philosophical science'. He calls knowledge that God makes known 'revelation'. His answer gives two different reasons for revelation. Read them side by side.

cases.label: Reason 1: truths beyond reason
cases.text: Aquinas holds that people are directed to God 'as to an end that surpasses the grasp of his reason'. You have to know a goal before you can aim your thoughts and actions at it. If the goal lies beyond what reason can reach, reason alone can never supply it. So some truths 'which exceed human reason' must be revealed. Without revelation they would not be known at all.

cases.label: Reason 2: truths reason could reach, but badly
cases.text: Some truths about God are within reason's reach in principle. Left to reason alone, though, they would be known 'by a few', only 'after a long time', and 'with the admixture of many errors'. Aquinas holds that salvation, which for him means reaching God as life's final goal, depends on this knowledge. So he says these truths too should be revealed, so that people learn them 'more fitly and more surely'.

activities.takeaway: Reason 1 is about truths reason cannot reach at all. Reason 2 is about truths reason can reach, but too rarely, too slowly, and too unreliably. A truth can need revelation for either reason.

activities.title: Which reason applies?
activities.prompt: Sort each truth by the reason Aquinas would give for revealing it. Some cards draw on the text, and their location is given. Cards marked 'Made-up case' are invented to illustrate and are not from the paper.

groups.label: Reachable by reason, but only for a few, late, with errors (Reason 2)

cards.text: What God has prepared for those who wait for Him, which 'the eye hath not seen' (Article 1, quoting Isaiah)
cards.feedback: Beyond reason. Aquinas uses this verse to show that our final goal surpasses the grasp of reason, so reason could never find it alone.

cards.text: Things 'shown to thee above the understanding of man' (Article 1, Reply to Objection 1)
cards.feedback: Beyond reason. 'Above the understanding of man' is exactly Reason 1. Such things can only be accepted by faith once God reveals them.

cards.text: What philosophers knew of God 'through creatures' (Article 6)
cards.feedback: Reachable by reason. Philosophers did reach these truths by reasoning from the world. That is why they belong to Reason 2, not Reason 1. Reason can get there, but in Aquinas's view only some people do, slowly, and with mistakes.

cards.text: God as 'known to Himself alone and revealed to others' (Article 6)
cards.feedback: Beyond reason. What God alone knows of Himself is, by definition, out of reason's reach. People can have it only if it is revealed.

cards.text: Made-up case: a truth about God that one gifted thinker works out after decades of study, still mixed with a few mistakes
cards.feedback: Reachable but hard. This case shows all three of Aquinas's worries at once: few people (one thinker), late (decades), and with errors. Reason did reach it, so this is Reason 2.

cards.text: Made-up case: a truth about God that no amount of careful reasoning, by anyone, could ever arrive at
cards.feedback: Beyond reason. If no reasoning could ever reach it, then being slow or rare is not the issue. It is simply out of reach, which is Reason 1.

activities.takeaway: Ask one question: could reason reach this truth at all? If not, it falls under Reason 1. If it could, but only for a few, late and with errors, it falls under Reason 2.

activities.question: Which passage states the second reason: that truths reason could reach would still be reached poorly without revelation?

options.quote: because the truth about God such as reason could discover, would only be known by a few, and that after a long time, and with the admixture of many errors.
options.feedback: Correct. This is Reason 2. The truth is one reason 'could discover', yet it would be known by few, late, and with many errors.

options.quote: Firstly, indeed, because man is directed to God, as to an end that surpasses the grasp of his reason
options.feedback: This is Reason 1. It is about a goal that 'surpasses the grasp' of reason. Reason 2 is about truths reason can grasp, but poorly.

options.quote: Although those things which are beyond man's knowledge may not be sought for by man through his reason, nevertheless, once they are revealed by God, they must be accepted by faith.
options.feedback: This is Aquinas's reply to Objection 1, about things 'beyond man's knowledge'. That makes it Reason 1 territory. It says nothing about truths reason reaches only slowly or with errors.

options.quote: But whatever is not above reason is fully treated of in philosophical science. Therefore any other knowledge besides philosophical science is superfluous.
options.feedback: This is Objection 1, the view Aquinas argues against. Reason 2 is his answer to it: even truths 'not above reason' are not adequately known through philosophy alone.

concepts.title: Sciences differ by how they know
concepts.idea: Two sciences can reach the same conclusion and still be different sciences, because a science is defined by its means of knowing, not by its conclusions.

terms.means: The route a science takes to reach its conclusions, such as mathematics, the study of matter, or revelation
The part of philosophy that studies God using human reason alone (Aristotle called it the divine science)

concepts.recap: A science is marked by its route to knowledge, so reason and revelation can be different sciences even where they agree.

understand.explanation: Objection 2 of Article 1 argued that philosophy already studies everything, even God, so no further knowledge is needed. Aquinas replies that a science is defined not by the conclusions it reaches but by its means of knowing: the route it takes to get there. His example is that the astronomer proves the earth is round by mathematics that sets matter aside, while the physicist proves the same thing by studying matter itself. In the same way, philosophical theology reaches truths about God by natural reason, while sacred doctrine reaches them by revelation. So even where the two overlap, Aquinas says the theology inside sacred doctrine "differs in kind" from the theology that is part of philosophy. This is Aquinas's own argument by analogy, and readers still debate whether the analogy fully holds.
understand.quote: Sciences are differentiated according to the various means through which knowledge is obtained. For the astronomer and the physicist both may prove the same conclusion: that the earth, for instance, is round: the astronomer by means of mathematics (i.e. abstracting from matter), but the physicist by means of matter itself.

activities.prompt: Two experts both arrive at the same conclusion: the earth is round. Look at how each one gets there.

cases.label: The astronomer
cases.text: Proves the earth is round by mathematics. In Aquinas's words, the astronomer reasons by "abstracting from matter": shapes and quantities are considered, and what things are made of is set aside.

cases.label: The physicist
cases.text: Proves the very same conclusion "by means of matter itself": by reasoning about material bodies and how they behave.

activities.takeaway: The conclusion is identical, but the route differs. Aquinas calls this route the means of knowing. He says the route, not the conclusion, is what makes astronomy and physics two different sciences.

activities.prompt: Now Aquinas applies the same move to knowledge about God. Recall the objection: philosophy already has a part that studies God, so why would anything more be needed?

cases.label: Theology inside philosophy
cases.text: This part of philosophy studies God by human reason alone. Aquinas notes that it knows God "so far as He can be known through creatures just as philosophers knew Him." This is philosophical theology.

cases.label: Theology inside sacred doctrine
cases.text: This studies God by revelation. It covers what reason could reach, and also God "as far as He is known to Himself alone and revealed to others."

activities.takeaway: Even where the two reach the same truths about God, their means of knowing differ. So Aquinas concludes that the theology in sacred doctrine "differs in kind" from philosophical theology, just as astronomy differs from physics.

activities.title: Which route reaches it?
activities.prompt: Using only what Aquinas says in this question, sort each claim by the route that reaches it: natural reason only, revelation only, or both routes, so that the same conclusion is reached two ways.

cards.feedback: Two sciences prove this, and both work by natural reason: the astronomer through mathematics, the physicist through matter. Different routes do not always mean reason versus revelation. Here they are two routes within reason itself.

cards.text: God is the highest cause of the whole universe.
cards.feedback: In Article 6 Aquinas says philosophers knew God as the highest cause "through creatures". Sacred doctrine also treats God as the highest cause. It is one conclusion reached by two routes, like the round earth.

cards.text: Something of God can be known from the things he has made.
cards.feedback: Philosophers reached this by reasoning from creatures. Aquinas also cites Scripture saying it: "That which is known of God is manifest in them" (Romans 1:19). A revealed text affirms what reason can reach, so both routes arrive at it.

cards.text: What God has prepared for those who wait for him.
cards.feedback: Aquinas quotes Isaiah 64:4 ("The eye hath not seen...") to show that man's end "surpasses the grasp of his reason." Truths like this "exceed human reason" and must be made known by revelation.
This is one of the articles of faith, the principles of sacred doctrine. Aquinas holds that such articles are received by revelation and are not proved by natural reason.

cards.text: The truths about God that reason could discover, though only a few would find them, after a long time and with errors.
cards.feedback: Aquinas says that even these were taught by revelation, so that salvation would come "more fitly and more surely." Reason can reach them, and revelation also teaches them. That overlap is exactly why he needs the idea that sciences differ by route.

hints: Ask first: could a philosopher with no Scripture reach this? Then ask: does Aquinas say revelation teaches it?
Two different routes can both be natural reason, as with the astronomer and the physicist.
Aquinas says truths about God that reason can reach were also revealed, so those belong in the overlap.
activities.takeaway: The "both" pile is the key one. These conclusions are shared by philosophical theology and sacred doctrine, and they show why sharing a conclusion does not make two sciences one. This sorting follows Aquinas's own view. Which truths about God reason can really reach is a question philosophers have long disputed.

concepts.title: Every science argues from its principles, not to them
concepts.idea: A science does not prove its own starting principles; it reasons from them to new conclusions and, against someone who concedes nothing, can only answer objections.

terms.means: The starting points a science takes as given and reasons from, rather than proving them inside that science
The core beliefs of the Christian creed, such as Christ's resurrection, which Aquinas treats as theology's principles
A strict proof that forces its conclusion from premises both sides accept
For Aquinas, the highest branch of philosophy, which studies being as such

concepts.recap: Proof starts from principles and does not end in them: theology argues from shared articles of faith, and against someone who shares none it can only answer objections.

understand.explanation: In Article 8, Aquinas says no science proves its own principles: it takes them as given and reasons from them to new conclusions, the way Paul reasons from Christ's resurrection to the resurrection of everyone. So arguing only works where the two sides share some starting point. With a heretic who accepts some of scripture, you can argue from the parts he accepts. With someone who accepts nothing of revelation, you cannot prove the articles of faith at all; you can only show that his objections fail, just as metaphysics, the highest branch of philosophy, can only answer the objections of an opponent who concedes nothing. Aquinas adds that such objections can never be a demonstration, a strict proof, but this rests on his own premise that faith is infallibly true, which the objector does not share.
understand.quote: As other sciences do not argue in proof of their principles, but argue from their principles to demonstrate other truths in these sciences: so this doctrine does not argue in proof of its principles, which are the articles of faith, but from them it goes on to prove something else

activities.prompt: An argument can do two different things with a starting point. Compare them.

cases.label: Arguing TO a starting point
cases.text: You try to prove the starting point itself. Aquinas says no science does this for its own starting points, which he calls its principles. A science leaves the defence of its principles to someone else, or to no one, and does not prove them inside itself.

cases.label: Arguing FROM a starting point
cases.text: You take the starting point as given and draw new conclusions from it. Aquinas's example: Paul takes Christ's resurrection as settled. It is one of the core creed beliefs Aquinas calls articles of faith. From it Paul argues to the general resurrection of all the dead (1 Corinthians 15).

activities.takeaway: Every science moves from its principles to its conclusions. Principles are where a proof begins, not what it proves.

activities.prompt: Now suppose someone denies theology's principles. What happens next depends on how much he still accepts. Compare Aquinas's two cases.

cases.label: The heretic: accepts some revelation
cases.text: He accepts some texts of scripture or some articles of faith, but denies others. You share some starting points, so you can still argue. You quote the texts he accepts, or reason from one article he holds to the one he denies. A real proof is possible because it runs from common ground.

cases.label: The unbeliever: accepts none
cases.text: He accepts nothing of divine revelation. There is no shared starting point, so nothing can be proved to him. What remains is defence: if he raises objections against faith, you can show where they go wrong. Aquinas holds that such objections are never strict proofs, which he calls demonstrations. To him they are only difficulties that can be answered.

activities.takeaway: Agreement on some principles makes proof possible. With no agreement at all, you can only answer objections. Aquinas notes that metaphysics, the highest branch of philosophy, is in the same position against someone who concedes nothing.

activities.question: Imagine Maria. She accepts the Gospels as revealed and believes Christ rose from the dead, but she denies that the rest of the dead will rise. On Aquinas's account, what can a theologian do with her?

options.text: Prove the general resurrection to her, arguing from the articles and texts she already accepts.
options.feedback: Right. Maria is like Aquinas's heretic: she shares some principles. Aquinas says that against someone who denies one article you can argue from another, just as Paul argues from Christ's resurrection to the general resurrection.

options.text: Only answer her objections, since she denies a principle of theology.
options.feedback: That is the unbeliever case, where nothing is shared. Maria still accepts a lot of revelation, so real argument from that common ground is possible. You are not limited to defence.

options.text: Prove the general resurrection from pure reason, without appeal to anything revealed.
options.feedback: Aquinas says arguments from human reason cannot prove what must be received on faith. The proof has to start from revealed principles she accepts, not from reason alone.

options.text: Nothing at all: once someone denies any article, discussion is over.
options.feedback: Too strong. For Aquinas, denying one article leaves the others standing. Those shared articles are exactly what makes argument possible.

hints: How much does Maria still accept?
Aquinas: against those who deny one article of faith, we can argue from another.

activities.question: Imagine Sam. He accepts no scripture and no article of faith. He offers an argument that one Christian doctrine is self-contradictory. On Aquinas's account, what can the theologian do?

options.text: Prove the doctrine to Sam by reasoning from premises he accepts.
options.feedback: Sam concedes nothing of revelation, and the doctrine is an article of faith. Aquinas says there is then 'no longer any means of proving the articles of faith by reasoning.'

options.text: Quote scripture as conclusive proof.
options.feedback: Scripture only works as proof against someone who accepts it, like the heretic. Sam rejects it, so quoting it proves nothing to him.

options.text: Examine Sam's argument and show where it fails, without proving the doctrine itself.
options.feedback: Right. With no shared principles, the only move left is defence: answering his objections. Showing that his argument fails is not the same as proving the doctrine true.

options.text: Admit that Sam may have strictly proved the doctrine false.
options.feedback: Aquinas rules this out. He holds that arguments against faith 'cannot be demonstrations, but are difficulties that can be answered.' Keep in mind that this follows from his premise that faith rests on infallible truth, which Sam does not grant.

hints: Sam shares no starting point with the theologian.
Without shared principles, can anything be proved, or only defended?

activities.question: Why does Aquinas say every argument against faith can be answered rather than being a true proof?

options.text: Because faith rests on infallible truth, and the opposite of a truth can never be strictly proved.
options.feedback: Right. This is his reason in Article 8. Note that it is conditional on his starting premise: it convinces someone who already grants that faith is true, not an outsider who doubts that premise.

options.text: Because he had checked every possible objection and found each one flawed.
options.feedback: He makes no such survey. His claim follows from a general principle about truth, not from testing objections one by one.

options.text: Because people who object to faith are always uneducated.
options.feedback: Aquinas says nothing like this here. His point concerns the logic of truth and proof, not the character of objectors.

options.text: Because theology is allowed to ignore arguments it dislikes.
options.feedback: The opposite: he says the theologian should answer objections. He just denies that they can succeed as strict proofs.

hints: Look for a reason about truth, not about people.
What can never be demonstrated, according to Aquinas?

activities.question: Which passage most directly supports what the theologian can, and cannot, do with Sam, who accepts nothing of revelation?

options.quote: If our opponent believes nothing of divine revelation, there is no longer any means of proving the articles of faith by reasoning, but only of answering his objections — if he has any — against faith.
options.feedback: Yes. This states both halves of Sam's case: no proof of the articles is possible, and answering objections is all that remains.

options.quote: thus we can argue with heretics from texts in Holy Writ, and against those who deny one article of faith, we can argue from another.
options.feedback: This is about the heretic, who shares some texts. It fits Maria's case, not Sam's.

options.quote: Hence Sacred Scripture, since it has no science above itself, can dispute with one who denies its principles only if the opponent admits some at least of the truths obtained through divine revelation
options.feedback: Close. It implies that proof needs some shared ground, but it does not say what is left when there is none. The correct passage adds that answering objections remains.

options.quote: Since faith rests upon infallible truth, and since the contrary of a truth can never be demonstrated, it is clear that the arguments brought against faith cannot be demonstrations, but are difficulties that can be answered.
options.feedback: This explains why Sam's objections can be answered, but it does not say that proving the articles to him is impossible. It supports only half of the case.

concepts.title: A science on borrowed principles
concepts.idea: Some sciences take their principles on trust from a higher science, as music takes them from arithmetic, and Aquinas argues theology is a genuine science in exactly this way, taking its principles from God's own knowledge.

terms.means: The mind's own power to see that something is true without needing a proof
A science whose proved results serve as the starting points of another, lower science
The core revealed truths that sacred doctrine takes as its starting principles

concepts.recap: A science need not prove its own starting points. Music borrows them from arithmetic, and Aquinas argues theology borrows them, through revelation, from God's own knowledge.

understand.explanation: Aquinas sorts sciences into two kinds. Some, like arithmetic and geometry, start from principles known by the natural light of intelligence: the mind sees for itself that they are true. Others start from principles proved by a higher science: the science of perspective (roughly, optics) takes its principles from geometry, and music takes its principles from arithmetic. The musician accepts these on the mathematician's authority and is no less a scientist for it. Aquinas argues that sacred doctrine is a science of this second kind: its principles, the articles of faith, are established in a higher science, God's own knowledge shared with the blessed, and reach us by revelation. This is an argument by analogy made from inside a faith tradition. It shows that theology has the shape of a science only if you grant that this higher knowledge exists and was truly revealed, and that premise is exactly what a sceptic would deny.
understand.quote: So it is that sacred doctrine is a science because it proceeds from principles established by the light of a higher science, namely, the science of God and the blessed. Hence, just as the musician accepts on authority the principles taught him by the mathematician, so sacred science is established on principles revealed by God.

activities.question: Before we start, give your gut answer. A field takes its starting points on trust and never proves them itself. Can it still count as a real science?

options.text: No. A real science must prove everything it relies on.
options.feedback: This is a common intuition, and Aquinas's first objection in Article 2 makes much the same point. Keep it in mind: the next screens test whether any science actually meets this standard.

options.text: Yes, if those starting points were properly established somewhere else, by someone in a position to establish them.
options.feedback: This is close to the line Aquinas takes. Watch for what he thinks that 'somewhere else' is, and for the assumption the whole argument rests on.

options.text: Only if anyone could check those starting points for themselves.
options.feedback: This puts the weight on public checkability. Aquinas's musician example will test the idea: the musician does not check everything himself, yet we still call music a science.

activities.title: The musician and the mathematician

steps.text: In Article 2, Aquinas begins by sorting sciences into two kinds, according to where their starting principles come from.

Kind one starts from what the mind can see directly. Arithmetic and geometry rest on principles known 'by the natural light of intelligence': the mind's own power to see that something is true without a proof.
steps.result: Arithmetic, geometry: principles seen by the mind itself

steps.text: Kind two starts from results that were proved somewhere else. The science of perspective (roughly, optics) uses results proved in geometry. Music uses results proved in arithmetic. The science that supplies the results is called the higher science.
Picture the musician. He does not prove again the facts about number that his craft relies on. In Aquinas's words, he 'accepts on authority' the principles the mathematician teaches him.
Does that make music unscientific? Aquinas says no. Music's principles were proved, just not by the musician and not inside music. Music reasons rigorously from them.

Now comes Aquinas's move. Sacred doctrine sits where the musician sits. Its principles come from a higher science, which he calls 'the science of God and the blessed', meaning God's own knowledge, shared by those who see God.
steps.result: Theology is to God's knowledge as music is to arithmetic

activities.takeaway: Every science starts from principles it does not prove. The question is only where the principles come from: the mind's own natural light, or a higher science.

activities.prompt: Match each science to the place where, according to Aquinas, its starting principles come from.

pairs.feedback: Right. Music 'proceeds from principles established by arithmetic'. The musician takes them on the mathematician's authority.

pairs.target: The science of God and the blessed
pairs.feedback: Right. This is Aquinas's central claim. Sacred doctrine's principles are established in God's own knowledge and come to us by revelation. In Article 5 he adds that it takes them 'not from other sciences, but immediately from God'.
Right. Arithmetic is a science of the first kind. Its principles are seen 'by the natural light of intelligence', so it borrows from no higher science.

activities.takeaway: The lower sciences lean on higher ones in the same way, and Aquinas places theology at the end of the longest reach: its higher science is God's own knowledge.

activities.prompt: Trace the route by which, on Aquinas's account, sacred doctrine gets its starting points and then puts them to work. Some arrows are tempting dead ends.
activities.explanation: On Aquinas's account the principles start in God's knowledge and reach us by revelation. In Article 8 he says 'our faith rests upon the revelation made to the apostles and prophets who wrote the canonical books.' They become the articles of faith, and sacred doctrine argues from them to new conclusions, as Paul argues from Christ's resurrection to the general resurrection. The route through human reason is a dead end, because 'arguments from human reason cannot avail to prove what must be received on faith' (Article 8). The route through philosophy is a dead end too: theology accepts its principles 'not from other sciences, but immediately from God, by revelation' (Article 5). It uses philosophy only to make its teaching clearer.
hints: Start where the principles are first known, not where they are first argued about.
Aquinas denies both that reason proves the articles of faith and that philosophy supplies them. How do they reach us, then?

activities.question: Look back at your first answer. Why does Aquinas hold that a field built on trusted starting points can still be a real science?

options.text: Every science starts from principles it does not prove itself, and some, like music relying on arithmetic, borrow theirs from a higher science. Theology borrows its principles from God's own knowledge.
options.feedback: Yes. This is the heart of Article 2. The demand that a science prove everything it uses fails for every science, not only theology. Note what the argument assumes: it works only if a higher divine knowledge exists and was truly revealed. A sceptic who denies that premise would not be moved.

options.text: Faith makes the articles of faith self-evident to everyone, so nothing needs to be borrowed.
options.feedback: Aquinas does not claim this. Objection 1 of Article 2 points out that the articles are not admitted by all, and his reply grants that they are not self-evident to us. Instead he treats them as 'reducible to the conclusions of a higher science'.

options.text: Theology can prove its articles of faith by careful reasoning, just as a mathematician proves theorems.
options.feedback: No. Article 8 says theology does not argue in proof of its principles, and that 'arguments from human reason cannot avail to prove what must be received on faith.' It argues from them, not to them.

options.text: Theology covers the same subjects as philosophy, so it inherits philosophy's status as a science.
options.feedback: No. Article 1 says sciences differ by their means of knowing, not by their subject. Article 5 adds that theology takes its principles 'not from other sciences, but immediately from God'. Its status as a science rests on that higher source, not on sharing philosophy's topics.
